content: In the management of patients with atrial fibrillation who have one or more risk factors for stroke, the primary endpoint of the ACTIVE W trial was defined as the first occurrence of stroke, non-CNS systemic embolism, myocardial infarction, or vascular death. The efficacy of treatment was found to be less pronounced among patients who were naïve to Coumadin (warfarin), although the p-value for the interaction was not statistically significant. The benefit of treatment was primarily observed in patients managed at sites where therapeutic anticoagulation was achieved for more than 65% of the time. When analyzing data from atrial fibrillation trials, it is essential to separately evaluate outcomes in patients who were previously treated with Coumadin versus those who were Coumadin-naïve. Patients with prior Coumadin exposure are likely to represent a subgroup that tolerates the medication well, having effectively passed a bleeding stress test, and thus exhibit a lower rate of bleeding complications. Conversely, patients who experienced bleeding while on Coumadin would have already been excluded from the study population. This selection bias may explain why previously treated patients demonstrated better outcomes compared to those who were Coumadin-naïve. The majority of the reduction in adverse events in the ACTIVE W trial was attributed to a decrease in stroke and non-CNS embolization associated with Coumadin therapy. The pathophysiology of stroke in atrial fibrillation is believed to involve embolization of thrombi originating from the left atrium. The data from ACTIVE W suggest that platelet activation and its inhibition may not play a central role in the prevention of mural thrombus formation and embolization in atrial fibrillation. Coumadin was more effective in reducing the incidence of non-disabling strokes rather than disabling strokes. However, there was an observed increase in fatal hemorrhagic strokes, which are more likely to result in mortality. This may partially explain why Coumadin was not associated with a significant reduction in overall mortality in the study. One limitation of the trial is that it does not address whether the combination of aspirin (ASA) and clopidogrel would be non-inferior to Coumadin in patients who are Coumadin-naïve. Notably, 77% of the patients in the trial were already on Coumadin and tolerating it well, while the remaining 23% who were Coumadin-naïve did not appear to derive any significant benefit from Coumadin therapy.
